title: Denormalization & OLTP vs OLAP
html:
Denormalization deliberately re-introduces redundancy to make reads faster or simpler — trading write complexity and consistency risk for fewer joins.

Common techniques

TechniqueExampleKept in sync by
Stored aggregatecustomers.lifetime_value, posts.comment_countTrigger, application code, batch job
Duplicated columnorders.customer_city copied from customersTrigger / app
Snapshot of a value at a timeorder_items.unit_price (price when bought)Written once — not really redundancy
Pre-joined reporting tableOne wide sales_fact row per order lineETL / materialised view
Materialised viewmonthly_revenueREFRESH
Key point

order_items.unit_price looks redundant with products.price but isn't: it records a different fact (the price paid on that day). Order 106 paid 52000 while the list price is 55000.

OLTP vs OLAP

OLTP (transactions)OLAP (analytics)
WorkloadMany small reads/writes by keyFew huge scans and aggregations
SchemaNormalised (3NF)Denormalised star / snowflake schema
ExamplesPostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server for the appSnowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse, DuckDB
StorageRow-orientedColumn-oriented, compressed
FreshnessReal timeLoaded by ETL/ELT (minutes–hours)

Star schema

A central fact table of measurable events (sales_fact: quantity, amount) with foreign keys to dimension tables describing them (dim_date, dim_customer, dim_product). Dimensions are wide and denormalised, so queries need one join per dimension.

Do

Normalise first; denormalise a specific hot path after measuring, with a clear owner of the sync logic (trigger, job, or materialised view).

Avoid

Denormalise “for speed” up front — you pay forever in inconsistent data and complex writes.

When would you denormalize?

When a read path is hot and joins/aggregations are measurably too slow even with good indexes, for reporting/analytics (star schemas), or to cache expensive aggregates (counters). Accept the cost: extra storage, slower writes and code/triggers to keep copies consistent.

What is a star schema?

A data-warehouse design with one central fact table (numeric measures + foreign keys) surrounded by denormalised dimension tables (date, customer, product, store). Snowflake schema = the dimensions are further normalised into sub-dimensions.
